title: WHY CALLING AMNON’S OBSESSION “LOVE” IS DANGEROUS
paragraphs:
WHY CALLING AMNON’S OBSESSION “LOVE” IS DANGEROUS
Scripture used the word “love.” Then the story showed us what was hiding behind it.
There is a sentence in the Bible that should make every Christian uncomfortable.
Not because Scripture got something wrong.
Because human beings have become frighteningly good at putting beautiful names on ugly desires.
“And Amnon the son of David loved her.”
That is how 2 Samuel 13:1 introduces one of the darkest stories inside David’s household.
Loved her.
Those words almost sound innocent.
Tender, even.
Until you keep reading.
Then the bedroom door closes.
A woman says no.
A man refuses to listen.
Strength becomes a weapon.
Desire becomes violence.
And the same man who said he “loved” her suddenly cannot stand the sight of her.
That is why we need to talk about Amnon.
Because some of the most destructive things people do to one another begin with a sentence that sounds almost holy:
“But I love you.”
And perhaps the frightening question is not merely whether we can recognize Amnon in someone else.
Perhaps the harder question is whether some version of Amnon’s lie has ever lived inside us.
Not necessarily his crime.
But his distortion.
The belief that wanting someone intensely means loving them deeply.
The belief that our feelings give us rights over another person.
The belief that because desire hurts, desire must be obeyed.
The belief that another human being exists to satisfy something aching inside us.
Scripture refuses to let that lie survive.
The Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 13:1 says of Amnon:
וַיֶּאֱהָבֶהָ אַמְנוֹן בֶּן־דָּוִד
Vayye’ehaveha Amnon ben-David.
“And Amnon son of David loved her.”
The verb comes from אָהַב — ’ahav — the normal Hebrew verb “to love.”
That matters.
We should not rewrite the verse simply because we already know how horrifying the story becomes.
The narrator tells us Amnon “loved” Tamar.
Amnon himself later says:
אֶת־תָּמָר אֲחוֹת אַבְשָׁלֹם אָחִי אֲנִי אֹהֵב
Et-Tamar achot Avshalom achi ani ohev.
“Tamar, the sister of Absalom my brother, I love.”
Amnon has a word for what he feels.
Love.
But having the vocabulary of love does not prove that your heart understands love.
Keep reading.
Because Scripture does something devastating.
It allows Amnon to call his desire “love”...
and then exposes that “love” by showing us what it produces.
Amnon becomes consumed with Tamar.
He becomes distressed to the point of sickness.
But notice where his attention is centered.
Not on Tamar’s flourishing.
Not on Tamar’s dignity.
Not on protecting Tamar.
Not on honoring God.
The gravitational center of Amnon’s world is Amnon.
What he wants.
What he cannot have.
What he feels.
What he needs.
And that distinction matters because biblical love is never merely measured by the intensity of the lover’s emotion.
It is revealed by what that “love” seeks for the beloved.
Amnon’s desire eventually asks a terrifying question without saying it aloud:
“How can I get what I want?”
Then Jonadab enters the story.
He is described as crafty.
And rather than confronting Amnon’s disordered desire, he gives it a strategy.
Pretend to be sick.
Get Tamar alone.
Manipulate David.
Create the opportunity.
Suddenly we discover another uncomfortable truth.
Sometimes the most dangerous friend in your life is not the person who hates you.
It is the person clever enough to help your sin succeed.
Some friends will help you pray.
Some will help you repent.
Some will tell you the truth when your flesh hates hearing it.
And some will help you arrange the room where your worst appetite can finally get what it wants.
Be careful who advises you when desire is screaming.
Jonadab gave Amnon a plan when Amnon needed repentance.
Tamar came because she was summoned.
She prepared food.
She served.
She walked into that room apparently believing she was caring for her brother.
Then Amnon ordered everyone else out.
The room emptied.
And the story changed forever.
He took hold of her.
He demanded that she lie with him.
Tamar answered.
No.
That word matters.
She pleaded with him.
She reasoned with him.
She called what he intended to do disgraceful and foolish.
She spoke about consequences for herself and consequences for him.
She was not unclear.
She was not inviting him.
She was not consenting.
She said no.
And Scripture tells us the devastating turning point:
“But he would not listen to her.”
Do not rush past that sentence.
Because that is where Amnon’s claim to “love” collapses in front of us.
Love listens.
Lust says, “But what about what I want?”
Love sees a person.
Lust sees access.
Love protects dignity.
Lust negotiates around boundaries.
Love can hear “no” and remain honorable.
Entitlement hears “no” as an obstacle.
Amnon was stronger than Tamar.
And he used that strength against her.
The Bible does not romanticize what happened.
It does not excuse him because he was emotionally overwhelmed.
It does not say his sickness made him innocent.
It does not blame Tamar for entering the room.
It does not suggest her beauty caused his wickedness.
The responsibility belongs to the man who refused to listen.
He violated her.
And then comes one of the most psychologically revealing verses in the entire account.
After getting the thing he had apparently been making himself sick to obtain, Amnon hated Tamar.
Not mildly.
The text intensifies it.
His hatred became greater than the “love” with which he had loved her.
Think about that.
Minutes earlier, his body had told him:
“I cannot live without her.”
Then after satisfying his desire:
“Get her away from me.”
That is not covenant love.
That is consumption.
And consumption always eventually becomes disposal.
This is why calling every powerful romantic or sexual feeling “love” is dangerous.
Intensity is not proof of purity.
Obsession is not devotion.
Jealousy is not automatically love.
Possessiveness is not protection.
Sexual hunger is not covenant.
Emotional dependency is not necessarily intimacy.
And desperately wanting someone does not give you a divine right to have them.
Our culture repeatedly tells people to “follow your heart.”
Scripture is far more suspicious of the human heart.
Human desire requires redemption.
Because without Christ, we are capable of baptizing selfishness with beautiful vocabulary.
“I love her.”
“I love him.”
“I need them.”
“They complete me.”
“I can't live without them.”
Maybe.
But ask a deeper question.
Do you want their holiness more than their availability?
Can you honor their boundaries when those boundaries disappoint you?
Can you seek their good when you receive nothing in return?
Can you accept “no” without punishing them?
Can you release someone without destroying them?
Can you love without possessing?
Can you desire without demanding?
Can you walk away rather than sin against God and wound another human being?
Those questions begin separating love from appetite.
And Christians cannot define love merely by butterflies, chemistry, attraction, sexual desire, loneliness, or emotional intensity.
We have a higher definition.
We have Jesus.
“Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.”
John 15:13.
Look at the difference.
Amnon says, in effect:
“I want you, therefore you must be given to me.”
Jesus says:
“I love you, therefore I give Myself for you.”
Amnon uses power to take.
Christ uses power to serve.
Amnon creates isolation so he can satisfy himself.
Jesus enters our isolation to rescue us.
Amnon refuses to hear Tamar.
Jesus hears the cries of the broken.
Amnon leaves shame on someone else.
Jesus bears shame He did not deserve.
Amnon gets what he wants and casts Tamar away.
Jesus receives sinners everyone else has cast away.
That is the difference between consuming someone and loving someone.
And maybe this is where the story becomes personal.
Because it would be easy to finish this article disgusted with Amnon.
Perhaps we should be.
But Scripture was not given merely so we could identify villains.
It was given to expose hearts.
Maybe you have never done what Amnon did.
Thank God.
But have you ever called control “love”?
Have you ever manipulated someone because you were terrified they might leave?
Have you ever used guilt to keep someone close?
Have you ever pushed a boundary because you thought your feelings justified it?
Have you ever secretly resented someone for not giving you the affection, attention, relationship, intimacy, or response you believed you deserved?
Have you ever confused being wanted with being loved?
Have you ever stayed inside a destructive relationship because someone kept saying, “I only act this way because I love you”?
Hear this carefully.
Love does not become holy merely because someone calls it love.
Its fruit matters.
Its character matters.
Its relationship to truth matters.
Its relationship to holiness matters.
Its willingness to sacrifice rather than consume matters.
And if you recognize something ugly inside yourself while reading this, do not hide from Jesus.
Run toward Him.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God refusing to leave you enslaved to what is destroying you.
Bring the possessiveness.
Bring the lust.
Bring the pornography.
Bring the fantasy life.
Bring the manipulation.
Bring the jealousy.
Bring the secret messages.
Bring the emotional dependency.
Bring the relationship you know dishonors Christ.
Bring the wound that taught you to confuse control with affection.
Bring the shame.
Bring all of it into the light.
Because Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve our vocabulary.
He came to give us new hearts.
The Gospel says something far more beautiful than “try harder to love correctly.”
It says that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
The sinless Son of God entered our ruined story.
At the cross, Jesus bore sin's judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns from sin and trusts in Him receives forgiveness that cannot be purchased, cleansing that cannot be manufactured, and grace we could never deserve.
Jesus does not merely forgive what you did.
He begins transforming who you are.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
But grace never calls evil good.
Grace tells the truth about the wound so healing can begin.
And that means we must also talk about Tamar.
Because for generations people have read stories like hers while survivors quietly wondered whether God noticed.
He did.
Scripture remembers her name.
Tamar.
The narrative records her protest.
It records her reasoning.
It records Amnon’s refusal to listen.
It records her grief.
Her torn garment.
The ashes.
Her cry.
Her desolation.
Her pain was not invisible simply because powerful men failed her.
And if someone violated, coerced, manipulated, abused, or exploited you, what happened should not be renamed “love” simply because the person claimed to love you.
Someone's desire for you did not give them ownership of you.
Someone's emotional intensity did not sanctify their actions.
Someone saying “I love you” did not transform wrongdoing into righteousness.
God does not require us to call darkness light in order to forgive.
And forgiveness does not mean pretending evil was harmless.
Christ can heal without rewriting evil as good.
He redeems by telling the truth about evil and proving that evil does not get the final word.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by erasing Tamar’s tears.
Not by calling Amnon’s actions misunderstood romance.
Jesus rewrites stories by entering the wreckage with truth, justice, mercy, forgiveness, redemption, and resurrection power.
Perhaps someone reading this is still sitting emotionally outside a locked door.
Still carrying ashes nobody sees.
Still wondering whether what happened destroyed the possibility of ever becoming whole again.
Listen.
Your wound may be part of your history.
It does not have to become your identity.
Jesus is still writing.
Perhaps someone else reading this recognizes themselves not in Tamar’s suffering but somewhere closer to Amnon’s selfishness.
This could be mercy knocking.
Confess.
Repent.
Get accountable.
Cut off whatever feeds the darkness.
Stop blaming loneliness.
Stop blaming temptation.
Stop blaming the other person.
Stop calling bondage “love.”
Bring the truth to Christ.
There is forgiveness for repentant sinners.
There is transformation through the Holy Spirit.
There is another way to live.
There is another way to love.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows exactly what Jonadab looks like too.
That friend who always encourages compromise.
That private chat where sin becomes a joke.
That person who helps you rationalize what your conscience already knows is wrong.
That voice saying, “Everybody does it.”
Maybe your next act of obedience is not merely leaving a temptation.
Maybe it is leaving the counsel that keeps leading you back toward it.
Because the people surrounding your weakness can either help escort you toward repentance or help engineer your destruction.
Choose people who love Jesus enough to disappoint your flesh.
And become that kind of friend yourself.
When somebody confesses temptation, do not hand them a strategy for sin.
Help them find the cross.
There is something else haunting about Tamar’s story.
Amnon wanted Tamar until he had harmed her.
Jesus wants wounded people precisely when they think their lives have become impossible to love.
The Gospel reverses the room.
The rejected are welcomed.
The ashamed are covered.
The guilty who genuinely repent can be forgiven.
The wounded can be restored.
The sinner can become a new creation.
Not because sin was small.
Because Christ is mighty to save.
Maybe that is why this story hurts so much.

Because somewhere beneath our carefully managed Christian appearances, almost everyone knows what it means either to have been wounded by somebody's selfishness or to discover selfishness inside ourselves.
We need more than romantic advice.
We need redemption.
We need Jesus.
So before you leave this article, sit with one question:
When you say, “I love you,” does your love increasingly look like Christ?
Does it protect?
Does it listen?
Does it tell the truth?
Does it honor holiness?
Does it refuse manipulation?
Does it know how to sacrifice?
Does it know how to hear “no”?
Does it desire another person's good even when that good costs you something?
Because Christian love is not proved by how desperately you want someone.
It is proved by whether Christ is teaching you how to seek their good without making them your god.
Be honest.
Someone reading your words may realize they are not the only person still fighting toward the light.
Not because every sentence will be comfortable tomorrow, but because there are truths we need nearby when feelings become louder than Scripture.
Not because Gospel Warrior needs another statistic.
Someone may still believe jealousy proves devotion.
Someone may still be excusing manipulation.
Someone may still be sitting behind a closed door wondering whether God saw what happened.
And someone else may be one act of repentance away from refusing to become the person their unchecked desires are trying to create.
Tell them about Jesus.
Tell them there is grace.
Tell them repentance is possible.
Tell them wounded people are not invisible to God.
Tell them sinners can be transformed.
Tell them the cross is stronger than shame.
Tell them the empty tomb means our worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending.
Because Amnon's tragedy shows us what happens when desire demands another person sacrifice themselves for us.
The Gospel shows us Jesus Christ—the King who willingly sacrificed Himself to save sinners.
Never confuse those two kinds of “love.”
And remember this when the door closes, when desire screams, when shame whispers, or when your past tries to pronounce the final sentence over your life:
What sin tried to turn into your ending, Jesus can still meet with redeeming grace.
